title: How to be a Jewish Adult
desc: Do you ever feel like you could use a handbook for how to build a Jewish life? title: Faith in Harmony: Voice
desc: The most human of instruments, the voice, is foundational to so many spiritual experiences—in its presence and in its absence. This free program explores the role of human voices in uplifting scripture, song, and calls to prayer in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, illuminating a shared dimension of Americans’ faith in harmony.

title: The Art of Chagall
desc: Marc Chagall’s whimsical, colorful art blends dreamlike imagery with themes from his Russian-Jewish heritage. A leading figure of the École de Paris, he worked across painting, illustration, stained glass, ceramics, tapestries, prints, and stage design. Art historian Joseph Paul Cassar examines Chagall’s life, artistic development, autobiography, persecution as a “degenerate artist,” American years, and major works, including the Paris Opera ceiling, Knesset tapestries, and renowned stained-glass windows. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: America's Sweet Tooth: 250 Years of Sweets, Treats, and Traditions
desc: What can pie, candy bars, and chocolate chip cookies reveal about American history? Food historian Francine Segan explores how desserts reflect the nation’s past, from English-inspired pies to modern social media trends. She examines how invention and necessity shaped sweets such as jelly beans and candy corn, how Depression-era scarcity led home cooks to ingenious recipes like “water pie,” and also uncovers truths behind familiar names and dessert myths—from Betty Crocker (not a real person) to German chocolate cake (not German). Registrants receive a companion recipe handout.

title: AI and the Humanities
desc: The words “Artificial Intelligence” now appear thousands of times per day. AI affects the global economy, jobs, medicine, national security, and more. Public humanities scholar Clay Jenkinson examines questions arising at the intersection of the humanities and AI: Will it revive engagement with great books or diminish it? How will schools adapt to the AI revolution? Using Hamlet , The Odyssey , and Crime and Punishment , Jenkinson shows how AI can deepen students’ engagement with literature.

This session focuses on the Newburgh Conspiracy.

Nurnberger traces its history, including the debate over transferring control to Panama, while examining why the United States built a canal in another country and why Panama was selected.

title: The Grateful Dead and the Quest for Transcendence
desc: The Grateful Dead has more than music to share: The band offers lessons on impermanence, interconnection, and the search for meaning, which author Casey Rae explores. Tracing the Grateful Dead’s connections to the Beat generation, psychedelia, and Eastern philosophy, Rae examines how the band’s music, community, and improvisational ethos reflect deeper questions about transcendence, identity, and human connection. title: The Mosaics of Ravenna: A Glittering Vision in Glass and Gold
desc: Once a capital of the Western Roman Empire, the Ostrogothic Kingdom, and the Byzantine Exarchate, Ravenna is famed for its dazzling 5th- and 6th-century mosaics. These masterpieces, found in UNESCO-listed sites such as San Vitale and the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, illuminate early Christian art. In this richly illustrated lecture, Columbia University art historian Sophia D’Addio explores their artistic innovations, symbolism, patrons, and enduring legacy. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis: Re-examining a Moment of Extreme Danger
desc: Most Americans know the basic story of the Cuban Missile Crisis: In 1962, the Soviet Union secretly placed nuclear missiles in Cuba, the United States discovered them, and after a tense 13-day standoff, the Soviets backed down. The episode is often cited as a model of effective crisis management. However, historian Allen Pietrobon revisits the crisis to argue that it was less a triumph of leadership than a near-disaster averted largely by luck and fear.

title: The Irrepressible Rosa Bonheur: “The 19th Century’s Most Famous Woman Artist”
desc: French artist Rosa Bonheur was one of the 19th century’s most celebrated animal painters. The first woman awarded France’s Legion of Honor, she gained international fame for her highly realistic works and dedication to studying animals firsthand—including at Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West Show. Known for her unconventional lifestyle (trousers, short hair, and smoking in public), Bonheur remains a compelling figure. In an illustrated lecture, art historian Nancy G. Heller examines her life, art, and lasting influence. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: How to Listen to Jazz
desc: Listening to jazz is a skill that can be developed through active listening. Educator and jazz musician Alan Sherwin explains that jazz is not random improvisation but music built on an underlying harmonic structure. Understanding these musical “rules” can reveal the order, beauty, and excitement within a performance. Using familiar songs by leading jazz artists, Sherwin introduces song form, the role of improvisation, and how musicians interact within a jazz ensemble to create the music listeners hear.

title: Justice on Trial: The Dreyfus Affair and the Making of Modern France
desc: Historian and author Alexander Mikaberidze explores the Dreyfus Affair, the case that profoundly shaped modern French political culture. Beginning with the wrongful conviction of Jewish army officer Alfred Dreyfus in 1894, he traces how the controversy exposed divisions over justice, authority, nationalism, religion, and citizenship. Mikaberidze highlights the role of antisemitism, Émile Zola and the rise of intellectual activism, and the political struggles that reshaped the French Republic, leaving a legacy for civil rights, press freedom, democratic accountability, and the rule of law.

title: “Keep Calm and Carry On": England's Home Front in World War II
desc: British government propaganda dubbed World War II “The People’s War.” Historian Julie Taddeo looks at the many ways in which civilians participated in the war effort, from the Home Guard volunteers of “Dad’s Army” to housewives who were reminded to “Make Do and Mend,” to child evacuees and those raising rabbits and collecting scrap metal. She also discusses how memories of World War II live on in British TV shows and films in the 21st century.

title: The Fairies of Winter: From Nisser to Huldufolk
desc: While most people think of fairies as small, sweet, human-shaped beings with butterfly wings who grant wishes, folklorists say that this tiny, sparkling version is a relatively new idea, and that, in fact, the fairies of older traditions are something much stranger. Among the most compelling are the fairies of winter. Folklorists Sara Cleto and Brittany Warman explore winter fairies from different cultures, including some who love porridge and one who will suck your breath away if she catches you alone on a mountain during a snowstorm.

title: Paul Simon's "Graceland": Days of Miracle and Wonder
desc: In 1984, Paul Simon’s new marriage was failing and his career was in danger of stalling. That summer, a bootleg cassette of township jive—the street music of South Africa—became his personal soundtrack. Simon grew determined to create a collaboration that included township jive musicians. The result was “Graceland,” which won two Grammys and sold 16 million records. Music historian Ashley Kahn unfolds the album’s history and impact, revealing Simon’s creative process, the controversies the music raised, and the forces that helped the album achieve mainstream popularity.

desc: The National Museum of Asian Art has over 46,000 artworks from across Asia. Enjoy some of the finest on a docent-led tour and learn about commonalities and differences in cultures, aesthetics, and ideas.

title: Tour | From the Louvre
desc: In From the Louvre: Masterpieces of Islamic Art , you can admire remarkable artworks created between the seventh and nineteenth centuries from a vast geographic area extending from Spain to India. title: Communal Shabbat Dinner: George Washington’s Letter to the Jews with Kesher
desc: Join us for a communal Shabbat Dinner with our Scholar in Residence, Charles Savenor. We will first enjoy a delicious meal together with new and old friends. Washington’s letter to the Jews of Newport, RI creates a precedent of equality unknown to Jews during centuries of exile. However, many questions exist about the 1790 document, including who actually wrote the letter and what our first president meant.
